title: 拆解中国的游戏外经济生态

Unpacking China’s Out-of-Game Economy
Skip to content
Weekly Digest
Unpacking China’s Out-of-Game Economy
By Mark Ma •   October 4, 2026
Source: Naavik
What is your game time worth? My answer is about RMB 7.29 an hour, a little over $1.
Fantasy Westward Journey is NetEase’s decades-old, turn-based MMORPG. Between January 23 and February 23 of this year, I made a total of RMB 1,028.95 (~$143) with 25 currency transactions, all on NetEase’s own trading platform Cangbaoge. After deducting game billing — namely, prepaid point cards for billing game time, which cost RMB 300 (~$42) — my take-home total was RMB 728.95 (~$101) across five accounts running side by side for 100 hours of my own time, an hourly rate of RMB 7.29 ($1+).
Source: author’s Cangbaoge records
Nothing about that month was illicit, and none of it happened out of NetEase’s sight. For an aged live-service product with an out-of-game economy around it, that economy could either be regulated into the sun or lost to third-party middlemen, neither desirable. Hence, NetEase built
Cangbaoge
to regulate its currency, item, and account trading, both to avoid losing its cut and to curb third-party scams. Every transaction incurs a commission of 8–10%.
Listings on this page run RMB 4,111–44,444 ($571–$6,173) | Source: Cangbaoge
The reason virtual item and currency trading could be made into an industry, albeit gray, is that items, gear, gold, and accounts all reside in databases owned by publishers, where they could be restricted, banned, taxed, monitored, or flagged. Human services, on the other hand, exist in gray-market shops, unaccountable to anyone but the workers. In China, the human services gray market for games employs
more than one million workers
.
Of course, in the West, Valve’s Steam Community Market works in a similar fashion with virtual goods, but that is a marketplace for items bolted onto specific titles. There was also the web3 gaming craze that led to all sorts of trading, but it completely fell apart due to weak games and poor economy designs. What is unusual about China is both the scale of virtual item sales and the size of the adjacent gaming human-services market.
Together, virtual item trading and human services form an out-of-game economy around games. The former is billable and often regulated and implemented by publishers themselves, whereas the latter remains fully gray. Juggling what’s controllable versus what isn’t has become a larger topic for Chinese publishers to sort out.
The Rise of Human Services
In the extraction shooter Delta Force, a human services gray market has emerged around its Operations mode — where players lose all looted items upon death. Because
player-to-player trading is unavailable
, an alternative economy emerged to fill the void.
Taxing these human services is nearly impossible for Delta Force given their gray-market nature. Outright bans are equally difficult to enforce: these third-party providers essentially function as in-game companions, escorts, or farmers, performing standard gameplay labor until an account actually transfers hands.
Such services
are categorized into three types
:
Green:
playing the game normally, at RMB 300–400 an hour ($42–56)
Red:
blatantly cheating, at 60% to 70% of green’s price, yet tripling the loot
Green performance:
resorting to cheating while concealing it
Roughly 70% of these service requests target specific maps known for lucrative item drops. Rather than utilizing in-game channels, third-party service providers predominantly market their offerings through WeChat mini-programs.
For instance, the third-party outfit Tianba Club
offers a currency-farming package priced at RMB 238 (~$33) for 12.88M in-game currency
, a substantial sum within Delta Force.
By comparison, Genshin Impact strictly prohibits both account transfers and player-to-player trading, effectively curtailing the trade of virtual goods while leaving human-provided services largely unaffected.
Big and Getting Bigger
The bigger half of China’s out-of-game economy centers on trading. The main forms of gray-market trading are gold sales in MMORPGs, account sales in live-service games, and item sales in extraction shooters.
According to
Guanyan Tianxia
, in 2023 China’s out-of-game virtual-item trading market drove a whopping RMB 74.25B (~$10.3B) in volume. This market has grown alongside China’s game market. In the first half of 2025, China’s virtual-item trading market was worth RMB 44.73B (~$6.2B), up 12.74% YoY, while China’s game market saw RMB 168B (~$23.3B) in revenue, up 14.08% YoY.
Notably, transactions conducted outside of games are a bit over a quarter of those conducted within them.
When we compare these figures to the RMB 3.34B (~$460M) generated in third-party account boosting services in 2023, it’s clear that boosting is a tiny sector of China’s gaming gray economy (less than 5% of measured transactions) compared to the goods-based market. In
that same time period
, gear, currency, and consumables accounted for more than 90% of items being traded on third-party platforms.
Source:
Guanyan Tianxia
, Naavik
It’s important to keep in mind that most of the boosting and other services being bought and sold don’t happen on third-party trading platforms where orders are measured and fees are charged. Jiaoyimao, for instance, charges 6% of the order’s value or a maximum of RMB 1,000, ~$139, whichever is lower. Since a large amount of activity happens in WeChat through mini-programs and other means that evade measurement, it’s impossible to say how large the business is there and how much the measured statistics undercount it.
Another gray market sector is
companion-play
, which generated more than RMB 10B (~$1.4B) in volume in 2024 — all of it outside publishers’ reach.
The Attempt to Control
Does all of this out-of-game economic activity eat into publisher revenue? The answer depends on who owns the marketplace for item sales, but publishers haven’t been able to tax human services
